claim: Plasmodium falciparum causes approximately 200 million cases of malaria and 600,000 deaths each year, mostly among African children.
source: Plasmodium falciparum is a mosquito-born parasite that causes approximately 200 million cases of malaria and 600,000 deaths each year, mostly among African children (WHO, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2014

claim: The most advanced malaria vaccine candidate confers only partial, short-lived protection in African children.
source: yet the vaccine candidate that is most advanced in clinical trials confers only partial, short-lived protection in African children (RTS, S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to RTS, S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2014

claim: Passive transfer of antibodies from malaria-resistant adults to children with clinical malaria results in a reduction in the levels of parasitemia and fever.
source: Abs play a key role in naturally acquired immunity to malaria as demonstrated by the passive transfer of Abs from malaria-resistant adults to children with clinical malaria, resulting in a reduction in the levels of parasitemia and fever in these children (Cohen et al., 1961).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 1961

claim: Individuals living in malaria endemic areas acquire protective antibodies but the process requires many years of repeated P. falciparum infections.
source: Individuals living in malaria endemic areas acquire protective Abs but the process is remarkably slow requiring many years of repeated P. falciparum infections (Portugal et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Portugal et al., 2013

claim: The inefficient acquisition of humoral immunity to malaria has been attributed to the extensive genetic diversity of P. falciparum parasites.
source: The inefficient acquisition of humoral immunity that protects from malaria has been attributed, in part, to the extensive genetic diversity of P. falciparum parasites (Takala and Plowe, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Takala and Plowe, 2009

claim: The inefficient acquisition of humoral immunity to malaria has been attributed to the extraordinary clonal variation in the proteins the parasite expresses on the surface of infected erythrocytes.
source: the extraordinary clonal variation in the proteins the parasite expresses on the surface of the erythrocytes that it infects (Scherf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scherf et al., 2008

claim: P. falciparum may evade humoral immunity through dysregulation of B cell responses.
source: However, accumulating evidence suggests that P. falciparum may also evade humoral immunity through dysregulation of B cell responses (Portugal et al., 2013; Scholzen and Sauerwein, 2013; Hviid et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Portugal et al., 2013; Scholzen and Sauerwein, 2013; Hviid et al., 2015

claim: P. falciparum-specific antibody responses are short-lived, particularly in children.
source: Indeed, several studies, particularly in children, show that P. falciparum-specific Ab responses are short-lived (Muller et al., 1989; Fruh et al., 1991; Ramasamy et al., 1994; Taylor et al., 1996; Cavanagh et al., 1998; Fonjungo et al., 1999; John et al., 2002; Akpogheneta et al., 2008; Weiss et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: P. falciparum-specific antibody responses boost inconsistently upon antigen re-exposure.
source: and boost inconsistently upon antigen re-exposure (Kinyanjui et al., 2007), even to conserved antigens (Fonjungo et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kinyanjui et al., 2007 and Fonjungo et al., 1999

claim: In areas of intense malaria transmission, P. falciparum-specific memory B cells are acquired inefficiently.
source: Moreover, in areas of intense malaria transmission, P. falciparum-specific MBCs are acquired inefficiently (Weiss et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2010

claim: The prevalence of P. falciparum-specific memory B cells is relatively low (∼30–50%) even among adults with documented malaria exposure.
source: and their prevalence is relatively low (∼30–50%) even among adults with documented malaria exposure (Dorfman et al., 2005; Weiss et al., 2010; Wipasa et al., 2010; Nogaro et al., 2011; Ndungu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: HIV and hepatitis C virus infection are associated with an increase in CD10−CD19+CD20+CD21−CD27− B cells that express FcRL4.
source: For example, HIV and hepatitis C virus infection are associated with an increase in CD10−CD19+CD20+CD21−CD27− B cells that express the inhibitory molecule Fc receptor-like-4 (FcRL4) (Charles et al., 2008; Moir et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Charles et al., 2008; Moir et al., 2008

claim: CD10−CD19+CD20+CD21−CD27− B cells are largely absent in the blood of healthy individuals.
source: cells that are largely absent in the blood of healthy individuals.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge following discussion of HIV and hepatitis C virus infection

claim: In HIV-infected individuals, CD10−CD19+CD20+CD21−CD27− B cells are hyporesponsive or 'exhausted'.
source: In HIV-infected individuals, these cells are hyporesponsive or 'exhausted', and because HIV-specific B cells are concentrated in this subpopulation (Kardava et al., 2014), they likely contribute to the humoral deficiencies associated with HIV infection (Moir et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kardava et al., 2014 and Moir et al., 2008

claim: An increase in a phenotypically similar subset of B cells has been described in malaria-exposed children and adults across genetically and geographically diverse populations.
source: An increase in a phenotypically similar subset of B cells has been described in malaria-exposed children and adults across genetically and geographically diverse populations (Weiss et al., 2009; Nogaro et al., 2011; Weiss et al., 2011; Portugal et al., 2012; Illingworth et al., 2013; Muellenbeck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: P. falciparum infection drives the expansion of atypical memory B cells, as suggested by a positive correlation between atypical MBC expansion and P. falciparum transmission intensity.
source: That P. falciparum infection per se drives the expansion of atypical MBCs has been suggested by a positive correlation between atypical MBC expansion and P. falciparum transmission intensity (Weiss et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2011

claim: Differential expansion of atypical MBCs occurs in age-matched children living under similar conditions in rural Kenya, with the exception of P. falciparum exposure.
source: the differential expansion of atypical MBCs in age-matched children living under similar conditions in rural Kenya, with the exception of P. falciparum exposure (Illingworth et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Illingworth et al., 2013

claim: Atypical MBCs appear in the peripheral blood of healthy adults following experimental P. falciparum infection.
source: and the appearance of atypical MBCs in the peripheral blood of healthy adults following experimental P. falciparum infection (Scholzen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scholzen et al., 2014

claim: VH and VL genes cloned from atypical MBCs from malaria exposed adults encode broadly neutralizing P. falciparum-specific antibodies.
source: Concerning function, Muellenbeck et al. (2013) recently showed that VH and VL genes cloned from atypical MBCs from malaria exposed adults encoded broadly neutralizing P. falciparum-specific Abs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Muellenbeck et al., 2013

claim: A study in Gabon reported that classical and atypical MBCs were different in their expressed IgG V gene repertoires suggesting that they developed from different precursors.
source: A study in Gabon reported that classical and atypical MBCs were different in their expressed IgG V gene repertoires suggesting that they developed from different precursors (Muellenbeck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muellenbeck et al., 2013

claim: A study in Mali indicated that the expressed IgG V gene repertoires of atypical and classical MBCs were remarkably similar suggesting a close relationship between the two populations.
source: In contrast, results from a more recent study in Mali indicated that the expressed IgG V gene repertoires of atypical and classical MBCs were remarkably similar suggesting a close relationship between the two populations (Zinocker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zinocker et al., 2015

claim: Atypical MBCs in Malian adults comprised 6–51% of total mature circulating B cells (mean 17.1% ± 8.2).
source: atypical MBCs in the adult subjects comprised 6–51% of total mature circulating B cells (mean 17.1% ± 8.2) compared to 0.6–8% (mean 2.9% ± 1.9) in malaria-naïve U.S. adults (p < 0.0001; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1C showing measurements from 107 Malian adults

claim: Atypical MBCs in malaria-naïve U.S. adults comprised 0.6–8% of total mature circulating B cells (mean 2.9% ± 1.9).
source: atypical MBCs in the adult subjects comprised 6–51% of total mature circulating B cells (mean 17.1% ± 8.2) compared to 0.6–8% (mean 2.9% ± 1.9) in malaria-naïve U.S. adults (p < 0.0001; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1C showing measurements from 37 U.S. adults

claim: The percentage of atypical MBCs is significantly higher in Malian adults compared to U.S. adults (p < 0.0001).
source: atypical MBCs in the adult subjects comprised 6–51% of total mature circulating B cells (mean 17.1% ± 8.2) compared to 0.6–8% (mean 2.9% ± 1.9) in malaria-naïve U.S. adults (p < 0.0001; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with p-value < 0.0001 shown in Figure 1C

claim: Naïve B cells are largely IgM+ while classical and atypical MBCs share an Ig isotype profile that is predominantly IgG+.
source: As expected, naïve B cells were largely IgM+ while classical and atypical MBCs shared an Ig isotype profile that was predominantly IgG+ (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from 7 Malian adults shown in Figure 2A

claim: The average number of cell divisions is similar between atypical and classical MBCs (atypical mean 5.4 ± 0.9; classical mean 6.5 ± 0.9; p = 0.24).
source: We found the average number of cell divisions to be similar between atypical and classical MBCs (atypical mean 5.4 ± 0.9; classical mean 6.5 ± 0.9; p = 0.24), whereas the number of cell divisions was predictably low in naïve B cells (mean 0.3 ± 0.7) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by KREC assay data from 6 Malian adults shown in Figure 2C

claim: The number of cell divisions in naïve B cells is low (mean 0.3 ± 0.7).
source: We found the average number of cell divisions to be similar between atypical and classical MBCs (atypical mean 5.4 ± 0.9; classical mean 6.5 ± 0.9; p = 0.24), whereas the number of cell divisions was predictably low in naïve B cells (mean 0.3 ± 0.7) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by KREC assay data from 6 Malian adults shown in Figure 2C

claim: Naïve B cell VH genes have low somatic hypermutation rates.
source: As expected, naïve B cell VH had low SHM rates, whereas classical and atypical MBC VH had similar SHM rates of approximately 3% for isotype switched clones (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by IgH sequence analysis from 4 Malian adults shown in Figure 2D

claim: Classical and atypical MBC VH genes have similar somatic hypermutation rates of approximately 3% for isotype switched clones.
source: As expected, naïve B cell VH had low SHM rates, whereas classical and atypical MBC VH had similar SHM rates of approximately 3% for isotype switched clones (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by IgH sequence analysis from 4 Malian adults shown in Figure 2D

claim: Naïve B cells are highly polyclonal.
source: Also as expected, naïve B cells were highly polyclonal, whereas classical and atypical MBCs had similar clonal expansion profiles (Figure 2E) and shared ∼10% of their clones (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by IgH sequence analysis from 4 Malian adults shown in Figure 2E

claim: Classical and atypical MBCs have similar clonal expansion profiles.
source: Also as expected, naïve B cells were highly polyclonal, whereas classical and atypical MBCs had similar clonal expansion profiles (Figure 2E) and shared ∼10% of their clones (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by IgH sequence analysis from 4 Malian adults shown in Figure 2E

claim: Classical and atypical MBCs share approximately 10% of their clones.
source: Also as expected, naïve B cells were highly polyclonal, whereas classical and atypical MBCs had similar clonal expansion profiles (Figure 2E) and shared ∼10% of their clones (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by IgH sequence analysis from 4 Malian adults shown in Figure 2F

claim: Atypical and classical MBCs are derived from a common precursor and differentiate in response to similar antigen-dependent selective pressures.
source: Thus, atypical and classical MBCs share similar isotype distributions, replication histories and Ig repertoire characteristics, which taken together, suggest that atypical and classical MBCs are derived from a common precursor and differentiate in response to similar antigen-dependent selective pressures.
evidence: Inference based on the combined data showing similar isotype distributions, replication histories, and Ig repertoire characteristics

claim: Principal components analysis of microarray data showed segregation of transcription profiles based on B cell subpopulation, but not age, gender or batch effects.
source: Principal components analysis of the microarray data showed segregation of transcription profiles based on B cell subpopulation, but not age, gender or batch effects (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by principal components analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: There are 1115 differentially expressed genes between atypical MBCs and classical MBCs.
source: Within-subject differences in gene-expression were computed and resulted in 1115 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between atypical MBCs and classical MBCs; 1082 DEGs between atypical MBCs and naïve B cells; and 161 DEGs between classical MBCs and naïve B cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis from 20 Malian adults

claim: There are 1082 differentially expressed genes between atypical MBCs and naïve B cells.
source: Within-subject differences in gene-expression were computed and resulted in 1115 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between atypical MBCs and classical MBCs; 1082 DEGs between atypical MBCs and naïve B cells; and 161 DEGs between classical MBCs and naïve B cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis from 20 Malian adults

claim: There are 161 differentially expressed genes between classical MBCs and naïve B cells.
source: Within-subject differences in gene-expression were computed and resulted in 1115 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between atypical MBCs and classical MBCs; 1082 DEGs between atypical MBCs and naïve B cells; and 161 DEGs between classical MBCs and naïve B cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis from 20 Malian adults

claim: 'PI3K Signalling in B Lymphocytes' is among the top canonical pathways that distinguish classical from atypical MBCs (p = 1.11e-5).
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) identified 'PI3K Signalling in B Lymphocytes' (p = 1.11e-5), 'Phospholipase C Signalling' (p = 1.08e-4), 'BCR Signalling' (p = 4.98e-4) and 'ICOS-ICOSL Signalling' (p = 1.41e-3) among the top canonical pathways that distinguished classical from atypical MBCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: 'Phospholipase C Signalling' is among the top canonical pathways that distinguish classical from atypical MBCs (p = 1.08e-4).
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) identified 'PI3K Signalling in B Lymphocytes' (p = 1.11e-5), 'Phospholipase C Signalling' (p = 1.08e-4), 'BCR Signalling' (p = 4.98e-4) and 'ICOS-ICOSL Signalling' (p = 1.41e-3) among the top canonical pathways that distinguished classical from atypical MBCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: 'BCR Signalling' is among the top canonical pathways that distinguish classical from atypical MBCs (p = 4.98e-4).
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) identified 'PI3K Signalling in B Lymphocytes' (p = 1.11e-5), 'Phospholipase C Signalling' (p = 1.08e-4), 'BCR Signalling' (p = 4.98e-4) and 'ICOS-ICOSL Signalling' (p = 1.41e-3) among the top canonical pathways that distinguished classical from atypical MBCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: 'ICOS-ICOSL Signalling' is among the top canonical pathways that distinguish classical from atypical MBCs (p = 1.41e-3).
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) identified 'PI3K Signalling in B Lymphocytes' (p = 1.11e-5), 'Phospholipase C Signalling' (p = 1.08e-4), 'BCR Signalling' (p = 4.98e-4) and 'ICOS-ICOSL Signalling' (p = 1.41e-3) among the top canonical pathways that distinguished classical from atypical MBCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Atypical MBCs show differential expression of several molecules involved in BCR and co-stimulatory signaling.
source: Consistent with the IPA analysis, atypical MBCs showed differential expression of several molecules involved in BCR and co-stimulatory signaling (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Atypical MBCs upregulate several inhibitory receptors including FcRL3 and FcRL5.
source: In addition, atypical MBCs upregulate several inhibitory receptors that are known to modulate B cell function including FcRL3 and FcRL5 (Figure 3D), members of the FCRL family that are preferentially expressed by B cells and possess tyrosine-based immunomodulatory function (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Li et al., 2014

claim: Other inhibitory receptors significantly upregulated by atypical MBCs include CD72, CD200R1, LILRB1, LILRB2 and FCGR2B.
source: Other inhibitory receptors significantly upregulated by atypical MBCs included CD72, CD200R1, LILRB1, LILRB2 and FCGR2B (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The differential expression of selected genes by microarray was validated by quantitative RT-PCR (r = 0.893; p < 2.30E-16).
source: The differential expression of selected genes by microarray (CD35 [CR1], CCR7, IL4R, FGR, LILRB2, CD11c [ITGAX], CD200R1, ALOX5, CXCR5 AND FCRL5) was validated by quantitative real time (qRT)-PCR (r = 0.893; p < 2.30E-16) (Figure 2E and Supplementary file 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 2E with correlation coefficient and p-value

claim: FcRL4 is not differentially expressed by atypical MBCs.
source: Of note, FcRL4, an inhibitory receptor that is upregulated on tissue-like MBCs and HIV-associated exhausted MBCs (Ehrhardt et al., 2005; Moir et al., 2008), was not differentially expressed by atypical MBCs.
evidence: Supported by microarray data and citations to Ehrhardt et al., 2005; Moir et al., 2008

claim: Malaria-associated atypical MBCs do not express FcRL4 at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Given the significance of FcRL4 as a marker for tissue-like and HIV-associated exhausted MBCs, we confirmed at the mRNA and protein levels by qPCR and flow cytometry, respectively, that malaria-associated atypical MBCs do not express FcRL4 (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: Supported by qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3F and 3G

claim: FcRL5 is upregulated by atypical MBCs at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: whereas FcRL5, an inhibitory protein prominently upregulated by atypical MBCs in the microarray experiment (Figure 3D), was confirmed to be upregulated by atypical MBCs at the mRNA and protein levels by qPCR and flow cytometry, respectively (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: Supported by microarray, qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3D, 3H, and 3I

claim: The surface expression of FcRL5 protein by atypical MBCs is bimodal, with approximately 40% of atypical MBCs expressing FcRL5 on average.
source: Interestingly, the surface expression of FcRL5 protein by atypical MBCs was bimodal, with approximately 40% of atypical MBCs expressing FcRL5 on average (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3I

claim: Atypical MBCs exhibit reduced phosphorylation of Syk, BLNK, PI3K, and PLCγ2 following BCR crosslinking compared to naïve B cells and classical MBCs.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed reduced phosphorylation of Syk, BLNK, PI3K, and PLCγ2 in atypical MBCs following BCR crosslinking compared to naïve B cells and classical MBCs (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from 8 subjects shown in Figure 4A

claim: BCR crosslinking induces robust Ca2+ mobilization in classical MBCs while Ca2+ influx is markedly reduced in atypical MBCs.
source: Similarly, BCR crosslinking induced robust Ca2+ mobilization in classical MBCs while Ca2+ influx was markedly reduced in atypical MBCs, a finding confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 4B) and flow cytometry (not shown).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Proliferation of atypical MBCs is reduced compared to naïve B cells and classical MBCs upon BCR crosslinking and stimulation with CD40-specific Abs, IL-10, IL-4 and CpG for 96 hr.
source: Indeed, upon BCR crosslinking and stimulation with CD40-specific Abs, IL-10, IL-4 and CpG for 96 hr, proliferation of atypical MBCs was reduced compared to naïve B cells and classical MBCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Atypical MBCs fail to produce IL-6 and IL-8 in response to BCR crosslinking and stimulation with CD40-specific Abs plus CpG.
source: Moreover, in response to BCR crosslinking and stimulation with CD40-specific Abs plus CpG, atypical MBCs failed to produce IL-6 and IL-8 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data from 6 subjects shown in Figure 4D

claim: Atypical MBCs do not produce CCL4 or IL-8 following 12 hr stimulation with LPS alone.
source: Following a12 hr stimulation with LPS alone, atypical MBCs did not produce CCL4 or IL-8 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data from 6 subjects shown in Figure 4E

claim: Malaria-associated atypical MBCs exhibit attenuated BCR signaling and Ca2+ mobilization that manifests as reduced proliferative capacity and cytokine production.
source: Thus, malaria-associated atypical MBCs exhibit attenuated BCR signaling and Ca2+ mobilization that manifests as reduced proliferative capacity and cytokine production.
evidence: Summary inference based on the combined data from BCR signaling, Ca2+ mobilization, proliferation, and cytokine production experiments

claim: In FcRL5+ atypical MBCs, the phosphorylation of PLCγ2 and to a lesser extent Syk is reduced compared to FcRL5− atypical MBCs.
source: We observed that in FcRL5+ atypical MBCs the phosphorylation of PLCγ2 and to a lesser extent Syk was reduced as compared to FcRL5− atypical MBCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from 7 subjects shown in Figure 5A

claim: FcRL5− atypical MBCs show diminished phosphorylation of PLCγ2 relative to classical MBCs.
source: However, even FcRL5− atypical MBCs showed diminished phosphorylation of PLCγ2 relative to classical MBCs (all of which were FcRL5−) (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from 7 subjects shown in Figure 5A

claim: A stepwise upregulation of inhibitory receptors leads to increasingly diminished BCR signaling, reminiscent of T cell exhaustion during persistent viral infections.
source: suggesting that a stepwise upregulation of inhibitory receptors leads to increasingly diminished BCR signaling, reminiscent of T cell exhaustion during persistent viral infections (Kahan et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on the observed pattern of BCR signaling attenuation and citation to Kahan et al., 2015

claim: A higher percentage of FcRL5+ atypical MBCs co-express the inhibitory receptor FcγRIIb compared to FcRL5− atypical MBCs.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that a higher percentage of FcRL5+ atypical MBCs co-expressed the inhibitory receptor FcγRIIb (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from 10 subjects shown in Figure 5B

claim: Atypical MBCs do not actively secrete antibodies.
source: However, we found that atypical MBCs showed no evidence of active Ab secretion (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ELISPOT data from 14 subjects shown in Figure 6A

claim: Atypical MBCs do not actively secrete antibodies during an active malaria infection.
source: With these fractions we found by ELISPOT that atypical MBCs do not actively secrete Abs during an active malaria infections (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by ELISPOT data from 10 children during acute malaria shown in Figure 6E

claim: Atypical MBCs do not differentiate into antibody-secreting cells when stimulated with CpG oligonucleotide, Protein A from Staphylococcus aureus, pokeweed mitogen and IL-10.
source: In contrast to classical MBCs, which readily differentiate into ASCs in response to these polyclonal stimuli, atypical MBCs did not differentiate into ASCs (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by ELISPOT data from 9 subjects shown in Figure 6F

claim: Malaria-associated atypical MBCs do not directly contribute to antibody-mediated protection from malaria.
source: Thus, malaria-associated atypical MBCs do not actively secrete Abs at rest or in response to a malaria infection in vivo. Moreover, atypical MBCs do not differentiate into ASCs when stimulated in vitro. Together these data indicate that atypical MBCs do not directly contribute to Ab-mediated protection from malaria.
evidence: Inference based on the combined data showing lack of antibody secretion and inability to differentiate into ASCs

claim: VH gene sequencing showed that VH gene usage and the rates of somatic hypermutation in atypical and classical MBCs are indistinguishable.
source: Indeed, VH gene sequencing showed that VH gene usage and the rates of SHM in atypical and classical MBCs, predicted to occur in germinal center reactions, were indistinguishable.
evidence: Supported by next generation sequencing data of VH genes

claim: A high degree of clonal connectivity exists between atypical and classical MBCs, indicating that a significant proportion share a common precursor.
source: Notably, we observed a high degree of clonal connectivity between atypical and classical MBCs, indicating that a significant proportion of atypical and classical MBCs share a common precursor.
evidence: Supported by IgH sequence analysis showing shared clones

claim: Atypical and classical MBCs appear to have undergone a similar number of cell divisions.
source: By KREC analysis we also observed that atypical and classical MBCs appear to have undergone a similar number of cell divisions.
evidence: Supported by KREC assay data

claim: Atypical and classical MBCs are closely related developmentally and have had similar antigen-driven germinal center experiences.
source: Together the results of these analyses suggest that atypical and classical MBCs are closely related developmentally and have had similar antigen-driven germinal center experiences.
evidence: Inference based on combined VH sequencing and KREC analysis data

claim: The differential expression of FCRLs by B cell populations may be dictated by the immune environment in which the cells arise.
source: These results suggest the interesting possibility that the differential expression of FCRLs by B cell populations may be dictated by the immune environment in which the cells arise.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that atypical MBCs express FcRL5 but not FcRL4, unlike tissue-like and HIV-associated exhausted MBCs

claim: Atypical MBCs have lost two key adaptive immune B cell functions: the ability to signal through the BCR and to differentiate into antibody-secreting cells.
source: Importantly, we provide evidence here that atypical MBCs have lost two key adaptive immune B cell functions, namely the ability to signal through the BCR and to differentiate into ASCs.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on BCR signaling and ASC differentiation

claim: The block in BCR signaling in atypical MBCs occurs at an early signaling event, the phosphorylation of the kinase Syk.
source: A direct test of the ability of atypical MBCs to respond to BCR crosslinking showed that signaling was blocked at an early signaling event, the phosphorylation of the kinase Syk.
evidence: Supported by BCR crosslinking experiments showing reduced Syk phosphorylation

claim: The block in BCR signaling is likely mediated by the several inhibitory receptors upregulated by atypical MBCs through their ability to recruit the phosphatases SHP1/SHP2.
source: It is reasonable to assume that this block is mediated by the several inhibitory receptors upregulated by atypical MBCs, including FcRL5, through their ability to recruit the phosphatases SHP1/SHP2 (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on known function of inhibitory receptors and citation to Li et al., 2014

claim: Atypical MBCs show reduced responsiveness to TLR4 and TLR9 ligands and other polyclonal stimuli.
source: Although here we observed that atypical MBCs showed reduced responsiveness to TLR4 and TLR9 ligands and other polyclonal stimuli, the extent to which this is modulated by FcRL5 expression remains to be determined.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on LPS and CpG stimulation

claim: Atypical MBCs do not spontaneously secrete antibodies from both 'resting' atypical MBCs in Malian adults and from atypical MBCs isolated from children during acute febrile malaria.
source: We observed a lack of spontaneous Ab secretion from both 'resting' atypical MBCs in Malian adults as well as from atypical MBCs isolated from children during acute febrile malaria.
evidence: Supported by ELISPOT data from both adult and pediatric subjects

claim: While atypical and classical MBCs appear closely related, atypical MBCs exhibit markedly reduced signaling and effector function, which may contribute to the inefficient acquisition of humoral immunity to malaria.
source: In summary, while atypical and classical MBCs appear closely related developmentally, atypical MBCs exhibit markedly reduced signaling and effector function, which may contribute to the inefficient acquisition of humoral immunity to malaria.
evidence: Summary inference based on all experimental findings

claim: In response to chronic malaria exposure, atypical MBCs appear to differentiate from classical MBCs becoming refractory to BCR-mediated activation and potentially interfering with the acquisition of malaria immunity.
source: Thus, in response to chronic malaria exposure, atypical MBCs appear to differentiate from classical MBCs becoming refractory to BCR-mediated activation and potentially interfering with the acquisition of malaria immunity.
evidence: Summary inference based on all experimental findings presented in the abstract
